1. **Idea:** The frames show a grid of columns, where each column seems to be a starting period. A lit square means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark square means the renter's invested pile was bigger. The point is that "rent and invest the difference" doesn't win or lose every time. The answer depends on when you start.

2. **What changes:** The grid itself barely changes. What changes is the on-screen text, which is added one label at a time. Frame 1 has "after the crash: lit again". Frame 2 adds "2009 to mid-2016: nearly 4 in 5 lit". Frame 3 adds "lit in stretches · one long dark stretch". Frames 4 to 6 keep all three labels, and the lit region at the right edge shifts slightly. The footer stays fixed: "US only · history, not a forecast". The top banner cites FHFA, BLS, Freddie Mac and K. R. French (CRSP), and a badge says "ILLUSTRATIVE".

3. **Meaning:** In US history, buying has come out ahead over ten years in many starting periods, but not all. There was one long stretch where the renter-investor came out ahead. Starts after the crash, from 2009 to mid-2016, favored the buyer in nearly 4 of every 5 cases. So whether the renter ends up ahead depends on the period, and neither side wins reliably.

4. **Advice:** The animation gives no direct advice, and there's no "buy" or "rent" instruction. A viewer would reasonably take away that the outcome depends on timing. They might also conclude that "rent and invest" is not a sure win, and that past results don't predict the future, since the footer says "history, not a forecast".

5. **Source of the takeaway:** The text on screen suggested the timing-dependence point. Those parts are the lit/dark legend, the "lit in stretches · one long dark stretch" label, and the "history, not a forecast" footer. The practical takeaway in 4 is my own inference. The animation never tells the viewer what to do. I also can't read exact percentages for any period other than the 2009 to mid-2016 figure.
